question.text: Krishna Real Assets Fund (Cat II) is evaluating whether RTA appointment is mandatory. Which of the following is the CORRECT regulatory driver that has made RTA appointment compulsory for AIFs?

answer.text: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 applied mutatis mutandis to AIFs
SEBI Merchant Banker Regulations mandating RTA registration
Companies Act, 2013 Section 88 registering beneficial interest

Amendments to the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 via Finance Act, 2019 (effective 1-Jul-2020) notified RTAs as 'collecting agents' for stamp duty on issue, transfer and sale of AIF units — making RTA appointment compulsory to enable collection of applicable stamp duty

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the chapter, the Central Government notified RTAs to act as collecting agents (amendments to Indian Stamp Act, 1899 via Finance Act, 2019, effective 1-Jul-2020). SEBI issued a circular confirming all RTAs registered under SEBI (Registrars to an Issue and Share Transfer Agents) Regulations, 1993 shall act as 'collecting agents' for stamp duty on issue, transfer and sale of AIF units. Hence RTA appointment is COMPULSORY to enable this stamp-duty collection. The Trap: The MF-regulations distractor wrongly imports MF regime. The Merchant-Banker distractor conflates with MB. The Companies-Act distractor cites beneficial-interest register which is unrelated to RTA mandatoriness for AIFs. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C tests the same stamp-duty-RTA link. XIX-A (Cat I/II Distributor) tests the LP-facing implication (stamp duty cost on subscription). XXI-B (Portfolio Manager) has separate PMS RTA requirements. Manager's Pro-Tip: RTA fees are usually % of unit capital + per-transaction fees. Negotiate a cap upfront. Also: ensure RTA has robust stamp-duty computation systems — Finance Act 2019 rates vary by state issuer location, and errors trigger investor-level demand notices.
